title: A Mummy With a Secret: Ancient Egyptian Held a Page from Homer's Iliad!
summary: Imagine wrapping a mummy and slipping a secret message inside — except the message is from one of the most famous stories ever told! That's what archaeologists discovered in Egypt. In a tomb at a place called Oxyrhynchus, they found a Roman-era mummy that's about 1,600 years old. Resting on its belly was a piece of papyrus with writing on it. Usually, when papyrus is placed on mummies, it has magical spells or prayers. But this one was different. Experts studied the fragile document and realized it was a passage from Homer's Iliad — a super-old Greek poem about the Trojan War. Specifically, it came from Book II, the "Catalogue of Ships," which lists all the Greek warriors heading to battle. Professor Ignasi-Xavier Adiego, who helped read the text, said this is the first time a literary work like the Iliad has been found used in a mummification ritual. Before this, only magical texts had been found in that spot. The discovery was made by a team from the University of Barcelona, which has been digging at Oxyrhynchus since 1992. The site is famous for preserving thousands of ancient papyri. This find shows that even in death, some Egyptians wanted to be close to great stories. Who knows what other surprises are still buried in the sand?
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that people long ago loved stories just like we do today, and it reminds us that great tales can survive for thousands of years, connecting us to the past.

background_read: Homer's Iliad is an ancient Greek epic poem that tells the story of the last year of the Trojan War. It was written down about 2,700 years ago and is still read today.
Oxyrhynchus is an ancient Egyptian town that was once a major city. Because of the dry desert air, thousands of papyrus documents have survived there for centuries.

Usually, Egyptians put magical spells or prayers on papyrus inside mummies to protect the dead. Finding a piece of literature instead is very unusual and shows that some people wanted to take their favorite stories to the afterlife.
Article_Structure: WHO: Archaeologists from the University of Barcelona, including Professor Ignasi-Xavier Adiego.
WHAT: They found a piece of papyrus on a Roman-era mummy that contained a passage from the Iliad.
WHERE: In a tomb at the site of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt.
WHY: This shows that sometimes literary texts were used in burial rituals, not just magical spells, and it gives a glimpse into what stories people valued.

perspectives.description: It's amazing that a piece of literature survived so long and ended up with a mummy. It proves that art and stories were valued even in death.
Some might say it was just a reused scrap of papyrus, not a deliberate choice. We can't be sure why it was placed there.
This find helps archaeologists understand that ancient Egyptians might have had a personal connection to the stories they read, unlike the standard religious texts usually found.
